questions.stem: An 8-month-old boy is brought in for the fourth episode of otitis media, along with two prior bouts of pneumonia and recurrent sinusitis, all beginning around 6 months of age. On exam, his tonsils are notably small and no palpable lymph nodes are found. Laboratory studies show markedly low levels of all immunoglobulin classes, absent peripheral B cells, and normal T-cell counts. A defect in which of the following is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: X-linked agammaglobulinemia results from a BTK defect that blocks B-cell maturation, leaving no mature B cells or immunoglobulins.
explanation.whyCorrect: The combination of recurrent encapsulated-bacterial infections after 6 months, absent tonsils and lymph nodes, low levels of all antibody classes, and absent peripheral B cells with normal T cells is classic for X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton agammaglobulinemia). Btk acts downstream of the B-cell receptor and is required for pro-B and pre-B cells to differentiate into mature B cells; without it, immunoglobulins are absent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes autosomal SCID with loss of T, B, and NK cells plus neutropenia, not an isolated absence of B cells with normal T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ATM mutation causes ataxia telangiectasia, presenting with ataxia and telangiectasias and a variable combined deficiency, not isolated absence of B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: AIRE deficiency causes chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis with autoimmunity, not agammaglobulinemia with absent B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A common gamma chain (IL2RG) defect causes X-linked SCID, in which T and NK cells are absent while B cells are present, the opposite of this B-cell-only pattern.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A male infant with X-linked agammaglobulinemia has a bone marrow examination as part of his workup. Pro-B and pre-B cells are present in normal numbers, but essentially no mature B cells or circulating immunoglobulins can be found. Which of the following best explains this arrest in B-cell development?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absence of a thymus preventing positive selection of B cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Accumulation of toxic purine metabolites that kill dividing lymphocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Failure to rearrange V(D)J gene segments in developing B cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of MHC class II expression on antigen-presenting cells

explanation.summary: Btk transmits B-cell receptor signals needed for maturation, so its loss halts development after the pre-B stage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Btk is a signaling molecule downstream of the B-cell receptor. Developing B cells must pass positive selection by receiving BCR signals; when BTK is defective, that signal is interrupted and B-cell maturation is prevented. Pro-B and pre-B cells are present but cannot differentiate into mature B cells, so peripheral B cells and immunoglobulins are absent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The thymus is the site of T-cell, not B-cell, development, and XLA is caused by a signaling defect rather than thymic absence.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Toxic purine metabolite accumulation describes adenosine deaminase deficiency, a form of SCID, not XLA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Failure of V(D)J recombination describes RAG deficiency, which prevents formation of both TCRs and BCRs, not the BCR-signaling block of XLA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Loss of MHC class II expression describes bare lymphocyte syndrome II, which impairs CD4 T-cell selection, not B-cell maturation.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A pediatrician notes that infants with an isolated inability to produce IgG typically remain healthy for the first several months of life, whereas infants with severe T-cell and NK-cell deficiencies often become symptomatic within the first weeks. Which of the following best explains why IgG deficiencies present comparatively later?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complement plays a greater role in immunity early in life than IgG

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgA and IgM fully compensate for the lack of IgG

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maternal transplacental IgG can persist in the infant

choices.label: D
choices.text: T cells secrete immunoglobulin in the absence of B cells in early life

choices.label: E
choices.text: The innate immune system can clear all infections without IgG

explanation.summary: Maternal IgG crosses the placenta and protects the infant until roughly 6 months of age, delaying the onset of antibody-deficiency symptoms.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that in XLA the age of presentation is early, typically around 6 months, because by that time the maternal transplacental IgG acquired before birth has degraded. Until then, this passively transferred IgG protects the infant, so isolated antibody deficiencies become apparent later than severe T-cell defects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The delay is due to persistent maternal IgG, not a special early role for complement; complement-fixing IgG and IgM are actually reduced in these patients.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgA and IgM do not compensate; XLA patients lack all antibody classes and remain vulnerable once maternal IgG wanes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: T cells do not secrete immunoglobulin; only B-lineage plasma cells produce antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The innate system alone cannot clear the encapsulated-bacterial and enteroviral infections these patients develop once maternal antibody is gone.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: Initial studies of a male newborn reveal an absent thymic shadow on chest radiograph, hypocalcemia causing tetany, an interrupted aortic arch, a cleft palate, and low-set ears. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: DiGeorge syndrome combines cardiac defects, abnormal facies, thymic aplasia, cleft palate, and hypocalcemia (the CATCH-22 features).
explanation.whyCorrect: A 22q11 microdeletion disrupts development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, which form the thymus, parathyroid glands, and great vessels. This produces the CATCH-22 picture: Cardiac anomalies, Abnormal facies (cleft palate, low-set ears), Thymic aplasia (absent thymic shadow), and Hypocalcemia from hypoparathyroidism, exactly as seen here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ADA deficiency causes SCID with lymphopenia and opportunistic infections, not the craniofacial, cardiac, and hypocalcemic constellation of DiGeorge.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ataxia telangiectasia presents in early childhood with ataxia and telangiectasias, not with neonatal absent thymic shadow, cleft palate, and hypocalcemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis presents in childhood with persistent Candida infections and endocrinopathy, not neonatal cardiac and facial malformations.
whyWrongByChoice.E: XLA presents around 6 months with recurrent bacterial infections and absent B cells, not with congenital cardiac or facial anomalies or hypocalcemia.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A neonate with DiGeorge syndrome develops carpopedal spasm and a seizure on the second day of life. Serum studies show hypocalcemia and an inappropriately low parathyroid hormone level. Which of the following developmental abnormalities best explains this metabolic finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aberrant migration of neural crest cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Accumulation of toxic metabolites in the renal tubules

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of the parathyroid glands by autoreactive T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Defective DNA repair in parathyroid chief cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Failure of B cells to receive T-cell help

explanation.summary: The 22q11 deletion in DiGeorge impairs neural crest-dependent development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, which give rise to the parathyroid glands.
explanation.whyCorrect: DiGeorge syndrome is caused by a chromosomal microdeletion at 22q11 that disrupts the protein responsible for neural crest cell migration. This causes aberrant development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, which normally form the parathyroid glands (as well as the thymus and great vessels). When the parathyroid glands fail to form, hypoparathyroidism produces hypocalcemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Toxic metabolite accumulation is the mechanism of ADA deficiency, not the parathyroid hypoplasia of DiGeorge.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Autoreactive T-cell destruction of endocrine glands underlies the hypoparathyroidism of AIRE deficiency (CMCC), not DiGeorge, where the glands simply fail to develop.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Defective DNA repair characterizes ataxia telangiectasia and does not account for the pharyngeal pouch defect in DiGeorge.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Failure of B cells to receive T-cell help impairs antibody production in DiGeorge but does not cause hypocalcemia.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 4-month-old boy has had persistent oral thrush, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, and failure to thrive. His newborn TREC screen was abnormal. Flow cytometry shows absent T cells and absent NK cells, while B cells are present but produce little functional antibody. A defect in which of the following genes is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: X-linked SCID from an IL2RG (common gamma chain) defect eliminates T and NK cells while sparing dysfunctional B cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The common gamma chain (encoded by IL2RG) is shared by receptors for IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, and IL-21. Loss of gamma chain signaling blocks T-cell development (IL-7) and NK-cell development (IL-15), so both are absent; B cells are present but dysfunctional because they cannot receive proper T-cell help. This X-linked pattern accounts for roughly half of SCID cases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ADA deficiency also causes SCID, but it eliminates T, B, AND NK cells and causes neutropenia, whereas here B cells are present.
whyWrongByChoice.B: AIRE defects cause chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis with autoimmunity, not a combined loss of T and NK cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: BTK defects cause XLA, which affects only B cells and spares T and NK cells, the opposite of this pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RAG deficiency leaves NK cells present while eliminating T and B cells, which does not match the absent NK cells and present B cells seen here.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 3-month-old infant with severe combined immunodeficiency is also noted to have neutropenia, sensorineural findings, and bead-like enlargements of the costochondral junctions on imaging. Which of the following immunodeficiencies is most likely, given that its underlying enzyme defect causes accumulation of toxic metabolites within lymphocytes?

explanation.summary: Adenosine deaminase normally clears metabolites produced during V(D)J recombination; its deficiency poisons high-turnover lymphocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: ADA breaks down toxic metabolites generated as a byproduct of V(D)J recombination. Cells with high turnover, such as lymphocytes, are especially vulnerable, so ADA deficiency leaves patients lacking T, B, and NK cells with neutropenia. It also causes nonimmunologic effects including the characteristic bead-like costochondral junctions from inadequate mineralization and cartilage overgrowth.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CMCC is caused by loss of AIRE and does not involve toxic metabolite accumulation in lymphocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DiGeorge results from a 22q11 pharyngeal pouch defect, not an enzyme that accumulates toxic metabolites.
whyWrongByChoice.D: XLA is a BTK signaling defect affecting B cells only, without metabolite toxicity or the costochondral changes described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: X-linked SCID results from a cytokine receptor (common gamma chain) defect, not from accumulation of toxic metabolites.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 5-month-old with recurrent severe infections is found to have severe combined immunodeficiency. Immunophenotyping reveals absent T cells and absent B cells, but a normal number of NK cells. A defect in which of the following is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: RAG deficiency blocks V(D)J recombination, eliminating T and B cells while sparing NK cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: RAG1/RAG2 perform the cutting and joining of V, D, and J gene segments. Loss of RAG prevents production of functional antigen receptors (TCRs and BCRs), so patients lack T and B cells. Because NK cells do not require rearranged antigen receptors, they remain present, distinguishing RAG deficiency from X-linked SCID (NK absent) and ADA deficiency (all lineages absent).

whyWrongByChoice.A: ADA deficiency eliminates T, B, and NK cells and causes neutropenia; it does not spare NK cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: AIRE defects cause chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, not an absence of both T and B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: BTK defects cause XLA, which affects B cells only and leaves T cells intact, not a combined T and B loss.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A common gamma chain defect (X-linked SCID) eliminates NK cells, whereas NK cells are preserved here.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 2-month-old with newly diagnosed SCID requires a red blood cell transfusion before hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. The team specifies that the blood product be irradiated and leukocyte-depleted. This precaution is taken primarily to prevent which of the following complications?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemolytic transfusion reaction from ABO incompatibility

explanation.summary: SCID patients cannot reject donor lymphocytes, so unirradiated blood products can cause transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick specifies that blood products given to SCID patients must be irradiated and leukocyte-depleted to prevent the immune cells in the products from attacking the recipient, i.e., graft-versus-host disease. Because the patient lacks functional T cells, transfused donor lymphocytes are not rejected and can engraft and attack host tissues; irradiation inactivates those donor lymphocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anaphylaxis from IgA deficiency is a separate transfusion issue addressed by washed products, not by irradiation to prevent cellular attack on the host.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemolytic reactions are prevented by ABO/Rh matching, not by irradiation or leukoreduction of the product.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron overload is a long-term consequence of chronic transfusion and is unrelated to irradiating a single unit.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cytomegalovirus risk is reduced by leukoreduction, but the stated reason for irradiation in the brick is prevention of graft-versus-host disease, which is the primary concern here.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl has had persistent Candida infections of the mouth, nails, and skin since early childhood. She has also developed hypoparathyroidism and is being monitored for adrenal insufficiency. Genetic testing confirms a deficiency of the AutoImmune Regulator (AIRE). Loss of AIRE most directly leads to her endocrine problems through which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absence of the parathyroid glands due to a pharyngeal pouch defect

choices.label: B
choices.text: Accumulation of toxic purine metabolites in endocrine tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure to express tissue-restricted self-antigens in the thymus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inability to rearrange V(D)J segments in developing T cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of the common gamma chain shared by multiple cytokine receptors

explanation.summary: AIRE drives expression of tissue-restricted self-antigens in the thymus for central tolerance; its loss lets autoreactive T cells survive and attack endocrine organs.
explanation.whyCorrect: AIRE allows medullary thymic epithelial cells to express tissue-restricted self-antigens, a process critical for central (negative selection) tolerance. Without AIRE, autoreactive T cells are not eliminated and escape into the periphery, producing autoimmune endocrine insufficiencies such as hypoparathyroidism (the most common) and adrenal failure. Loss of AIRE also reduces the PRR Dectin-1, explaining the chronic candidiasis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Absent parathyroid glands from a pharyngeal pouch defect describes DiGeorge; in CMCC the glands are destroyed by autoreactive T cells rather than failing to form.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Toxic purine metabolite accumulation is the mechanism of ADA deficiency, not of AIRE-related autoimmunity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Failure of V(D)J recombination describes RAG deficiency (SCID), not the autoimmune mechanism of AIRE loss.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Loss of the common gamma chain describes X-linked SCID and does not cause autoimmune endocrinopathy.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A child with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis undergoes an intradermal Candida antigen skin test, analogous to a tuberculin (PPD) test, to evaluate her cellular response. In a patient with this disorder, which of the following results would be expected at the injection site?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A large indurated area indicating a strong response

choices.label: D
choices.text: Necrosis identical to a positive tuberculin test

explanation.summary: CMCC patients mount little inflammation to Candida antigen because their T-cell response to Candida is defective.
explanation.whyCorrect: Candida species are environmental, so most people's immune systems respond to injected Candida antigen with a delayed inflammatory (DTH) reaction, just as a person previously exposed to Mycobacterium tuberculosis reacts to PPD. Because CMCC patients have defective T-cell responses to Candida (partly from reduced Dectin-1), they show little to no inflammation on the Candida skin test.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A strong indurated response is what a healthy, Candida-exposed person shows; the CMCC patient's defective T-cell response prevents it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A rapid wheal-and-flare is an immediate IgE-mediated (type I) reaction, not the delayed cellular response being assessed here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Necrosis mimicking a strong positive tuberculin test would indicate an intact, robust response, the opposite of the anergy seen in CMCC.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vesicles with lymphadenopathy is not the expected pattern; the hallmark of CMCC on this test is an absent or minimal reaction.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl has progressively worsening unsteady gait and clumsy movements first noticed before age 2. On exam she has dilated, tortuous vessels on the bulbar conjunctivae. She has had several sinopulmonary infections, and her parents recall a marked granulomatous reaction after a live rubella vaccination. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in a gene responsible for DNA damage repair and cell-cycle regulation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Ataxia telangiectasia results from ATM mutation and presents with ataxia, telangiectasias, sinopulmonary infections, and a granulomatous reaction to live vaccines.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ataxia telangiectasia is caused by autosomal recessive mutations in the ATM gene, which detects and repairs DNA damage and regulates cell-cycle genes such as p53 and BRCA1. Patients present with ataxia (noticeable before age 2), telangiectasias of the conjunctiva and exposed skin (by 3-6 years), and about half develop immunodeficiency with recurrent sinopulmonary infections and a granulomatous reaction to the live rubella vaccine, all matching this child.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CMCC presents with chronic Candida infections and endocrinopathy, not neurologic ataxia with telangiectasias.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DiGeorge presents in the newborn period with cardiac defects, hypocalcemia, and craniofacial anomalies, not progressive ataxia with conjunctival telangiectasias.
whyWrongByChoice.D: XLA affects boys and presents with recurrent bacterial infections and absent B cells, without ataxia, telangiectasias, or a DNA-repair defect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: X-linked SCID presents in early infancy with overwhelming opportunistic infections and lymphopenia, not with a slowly progressive movement disorder and telangiectasias.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 9-month-old girl has had Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, disseminated cytomegalovirus infection, persistent oral candidiasis, and two episodes of pneumococcal otitis media. Her weight has fallen below the 5th percentile. Based on the spectrum of infections in her history, which of the following components of the immune system is most likely deficient?

explanation.summary: The types of infections in a patient's history point to the cells affected: viral, fungal, and intracellular infections indicate a T cell deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Humoral deficiencies increase the risk of mucosal infections and infections with encapsulated bacteria. Patients with T cell deficiencies present with all types of infections, including those seen in humoral deficiencies plus additional viral, fungal, and intracellular bacterial infections. Pneumocystis, cytomegalovirus, and Candida infections alongside pneumococcal otitis therefore indicate a T cell defect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An isolated B cell deficiency causes pyogenic, encapsulated bacterial, and enteroviral infections, not intracellular and opportunistic fungal infections.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of mucosal IgA predisposes to mucosal and enteroviral infections but would not explain Pneumocystis, cytomegalovirus, or fungal infections.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of opsonizing IgG predisposes to encapsulated bacterial infections only; it does not account for the viral and fungal infections here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Waning of transplacental IgG occurs in all infants and causes a transient low IgG; it does not produce opportunistic viral and fungal infections.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with recurrent infections undergoes immunologic evaluation. Intradermal skin testing with common recall antigens produces no induration, and his lymphocytes fail to proliferate when stimulated with mitogens in vitro. A lymph node biopsy shows reduced T cell zones with preserved follicles. Which of the following complications is most characteristic of this class of immunodeficiency?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of germinal centers in lymphoid organs

explanation.summary: T cell deficiencies are defined by reduced DTH reactions, defective mitogen responses, and reduced T cell zones, and they uniquely predispose to virus-associated malignancies.
explanation.whyCorrect: The laboratory abnormalities of T cell deficiencies include reduced T cell zones in lymphoid organs, reduced delayed-type hypersensitivity reactions to common antigens, and defective T cell proliferative responses to mitogens in vitro. Their common infectious consequences are viral and other intracellular microbial infections and virus-associated malignancies such as EBV-associated lymphomas, which is the complication characteristic of this class.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enteroviral infections are listed among the consequences of B cell deficiencies, which lack neutralizing antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Absent or reduced follicles and germinal centers are the histopathologic finding of B cell deficiencies; this patient's follicles are preserved.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pyogenic infections with encapsulated bacteria are the characteristic consequence of B cell (and innate) deficiencies, not the defining complication of a T cell deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reduced serum immunoglobulin levels characterize B cell deficiencies rather than the T cell pattern described here.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: An 8-month-old boy with a severe inborn error of immunity has had five serious infections since birth. His weight has plateaued and is now below the 3rd percentile despite adequate caloric intake. Which of the following best explains his poor weight gain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absence of the thymus reduces growth hormone secretion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypocalcemia from hypoparathyroidism impairs skeletal bone growth

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immunoglobulin replacement therapy suppresses appetite and feeding

choices.label: D
choices.text: Persistent immune activation consumes energy that would otherwise support growth

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toxic purine metabolites accumulate in the growth plates

explanation.summary: Failure to thrive is a hallmark of severe IEIs because an inefficient immune system is metabolically expensive.
explanation.whyCorrect: One hallmark of a severe IEI is failure to thrive, in which an infant has poor weight gain. The immune cells that are still functioning use much of the caloric intake to fight infections, including longer-term infections, so that energy is not available for growth.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thymic absence impairs T cell development in DiGeorge syndrome; growth failure in IEIs is attributed to caloric diversion to infection, not to hormone deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypocalcemia from hypoparathyroidism is a feature of DiGeorge syndrome and CMCC, not the general mechanism of failure to thrive across severe IEIs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunoglobulin replacement is a treatment for antibody deficiency; the brick does not describe it as a cause of poor growth.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toxic metabolite accumulation is specific to ADA deficiency and damages lymphocytes; it is not the general explanation for failure to thrive in IEIs.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl with partial DiGeorge syndrome has a low CD3+ T cell count. Her total B cell count is normal, yet she mounts poor antibody responses to protein vaccines and has recurrent sinopulmonary infections. Which of the following best explains her impaired antibody production?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B cells cannot receive CD40L and cytokine signals from T helper cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bruton tyrosine kinase signaling downstream of the BCR is interrupted

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pro-B and pre-B cells fail to differentiate into mature B cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: RAG-mediated rearrangement of immunoglobulin genes is defective

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toxic metabolites accumulate in rapidly dividing B cells

explanation.summary: In DiGeorge syndrome B cell numbers are normal but their function is not, because effective humoral immunity requires T cell help.
explanation.whyCorrect: Effective humoral immunity requires that B cells receive T cell help in the form of CD40L and cytokines. When T cells are absent or dysfunctional, B cell activation and antibody production are inhibited. In DiGeorge syndrome, B cell numbers are usually normal but their function is impaired because B cells require T cell help for optimal antibody production.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Interrupted Btk signaling is the mechanism of XLA, which causes absent B cells rather than normal numbers of poorly functioning B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A block between pre-B and mature B cells describes XLA; DiGeorge does not affect the B cell maturation pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Defective RAG recombination causes SCID with absent T and B cells; her B cell count is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toxic metabolite accumulation is the mechanism of ADA deficiency and eliminates T, B, and NK cells; it is unrelated to DiGeorge syndrome.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 7-month-old boy is diagnosed with X-linked agammaglobulinemia after presenting with recurrent otitis media and pneumonia. His mother reports that her brother died of pneumonia in infancy. Which of the following best describes the inheritance and expected distribution of affected individuals in this disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autosomal dominant; an affected parent in every generation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autosomal recessive; affects males and females equally

choices.label: C
choices.text: Not inherited; arises as a sporadic microdeletion

choices.label: D
choices.text: X-linked recessive; affects almost only individuals with one X chromosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-linked recessive; affects almost only individuals with two X chromosomes

explanation.summary: BTK is on the X chromosome and mutations are recessive, so XLA occurs almost exclusively in individuals with a single X chromosome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The gene for Btk is on the X chromosome, and mutations are recessive. XLA is therefore almost exclusively found in individuals with only one X chromosome (usually, but not always, phenotypically male children). Patients are usually male and commonly have other affected males in their extended family, such as the maternal uncle here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: None of the IEIs in this group is described as autosomal dominant; XLA does not show affected parents in every generation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Autosomal recessive inheritance describes autosomal SCID, CMCC, and ataxia telangiectasia, not XLA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A sporadic, non-inherited microdeletion describes DiGeorge syndrome, in which no family history is expected.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Individuals with two X chromosomes are almost never affected, because a second X chromosome carrying a normal BTK allele compensates for the recessive mutation.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 10-month-old boy with X-linked agammaglobulinemia receiving immunoglobulin replacement develops hand-foot-and-mouth disease followed by 3 weeks of watery diarrhea. Deficiency of which of the following best accounts for his susceptibility to these infections?

explanation.summary: XLA patients lack virus-neutralizing mucosal IgA, so enteroviral infections such as hand-foot-and-mouth disease and diarrhea are common.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because XLA patients lack all antibody classes, they lack virus-neutralizing mucosal IgA in addition to opsonizing and complement-fixing IgG and IgM. The absence of mucosal IgA makes enteroviral infections common, with hand-foot-and-mouth disease and diarrhea given as examples.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lack of complement-fixing IgG and IgM predisposes to encapsulated bacterial infection and septicemia rather than enteroviral disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: T cell counts are normal in XLA; the defect is confined to B cell maturation and antibody production.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reduced Dectin-1 is a feature of CMCC and impairs defense against Candida; it is not part of XLA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lack of opsonizing IgG explains the recurrent encapsulated bacterial infections of XLA (otitis media, bronchitis, pneumonia), not mucosal enteroviral infections.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 7-month-old boy is evaluated after two episodes of otitis media. He was born to a mother with heavy alcohol use during pregnancy and has facial features consistent with fetal alcohol syndrome. Serum IgG is 310 mg/dL. Flow cytometry shows normal numbers of B cells and T cells, and tonsils are readily visible on examination. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy is diagnosed when infant IgG is below 400 mg/dL with normal B cell numbers; it is not a true IEI.
explanation.whyCorrect: All infants experience a period of low IgG as transplacental IgG wanes before intrinsic IgG production becomes significant. THI is diagnosed when the infant's plasma IgG is less than 400 mg/dL. It is not a true IEI but a phenomenon that may be associated with fetal alcohol syndrome or mineral deficiencies, and infants with THI have normal numbers of B cells, as seen here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ataxia telangiectasia presents with ataxia before age 2 and reduced TRECs; it is not suggested by an isolated low IgG in an infant with normal lymphocyte counts.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DiGeorge syndrome is a T cell deficiency with craniofacial and cardiac anomalies and hypocalcemia; T cell counts here are normal and the facial features are attributed to fetal alcohol exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: XLA presents with absent peripheral B cells, low levels of all antibody classes, and reduced or absent tonsils; this infant has normal B cells and visible tonsils.
whyWrongByChoice.E: X-linked SCID presents before 6 months with opportunistic infections and absent T and NK cells, not isolated low IgG with normal lymphocyte counts.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: Genetic testing confirms a BTK mutation in a 9-month-old boy with absent peripheral B cells and low serum IgG, IgA, and IgM. Which of the following is the mainstay of long-term management for this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enzyme replacement therapy and gene therapy

explanation.summary: XLA is treated primarily by immunoglobulin replacement, together with prophylactic antibiotics.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once XLA is confirmed by genetic testing, treatment is immunoglobulin (Ig) replacement and prophylactic antibiotics. Replacing the missing antibodies compensates for the absent B cells and immunoglobulins that leave these patients susceptible to encapsulated bacteria and enteroviruses.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enzyme replacement is used for ADA-deficient SCID until transplantation is feasible; there is no enzyme replacement for a Btk defect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the definitive treatment for SCID, not the standard management of XLA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immunosuppressants and endocrine replacement are additional therapies in CMCC for its autoimmunity and endocrine insufficiencies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thymus transplant is reserved for complete DiGeorge syndrome, in which the thymus is absent; XLA is a B cell disorder.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A lymph node biopsy is obtained from a 1-year-old boy with X-linked agammaglobulinemia during evaluation of a persistent infection. Which of the following histologic findings is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absence of B cell follicles and germinal centers

choices.label: B
choices.text: Depletion of T cell zones with preserved follicles

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hyperplastic germinal centers with plasma cell expansion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal architecture with reduced natural killer cells

explanation.summary: Histology in XLA shows loss of B cell follicles and germinal centers because mature B cells never develop.
explanation.whyCorrect: In XLA, peripheral mature B cells are absent while T cell counts are normal. Histology therefore indicates a loss of B cell follicles and germinal centers, consistent with the general finding in B cell deficiencies of absent or reduced follicles and germinal centers in lymphoid organs. Clinically this corresponds to the reduced or absent tonsils and lymph nodes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Reduced T cell zones characterize T cell deficiencies; T cells are normal in XLA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A granulomatous reaction is described in ataxia telangiectasia after live rubella vaccination, not as the lymph node histology of XLA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Germinal center hyperplasia and plasma cell expansion require mature B cells, which are absent in XLA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NK cells are not affected in XLA, and the architecture is not normal because follicles and germinal centers are lost.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 4-month-old girl with partial DiGeorge syndrome confirmed by 22q11 FISH has a hypoplastic but present thymus and moderately reduced T cell counts. She has required antibiotics for two episodes of sinusitis. Her parents ask about the expected course of her immune function. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A thymus transplant is warranted because the thymus is hypoplastic

choices.label: B
choices.text: B and NK cell counts will fall as T cell help is lost

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation will be required within the year

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immunodeficiency severity typically decreases as she gets older

choices.label: E
choices.text: T cells will progressively disappear as the thymus involutes

explanation.summary: In partial DiGeorge syndrome the degree of thymic hypoplasia sets T cell numbers, and for most patients immunodeficiency severity decreases with age.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with partial DGS have some thymic tissue and varying degrees of immunodeficiency; the degree of thymic hypoplasia correlates with T cell numbers and thus severity. Management of partial DGS includes antibiotics, antifungals, and immunoglobulin replacement depending on infection severity and frequency, and for most patients immunodeficiency severity decreases with age.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thymus transplant may be warranted for complete DGS (completely absent thymus), which affects fewer than 5% of patients; she has thymic tissue present.
whyWrongByChoice.B: In DiGeorge syndrome, B and NK cell counts are normal; only T cell counts are low or normal depending on thymic tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HSCT is the definitive treatment for SCID; it is not described as the management of partial DGS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick describes improvement with age in most patients with partial DGS, not progressive loss of T cells.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A newborn with a 22q11 microdeletion, an interrupted aortic arch, and hypocalcemia has no detectable thymic tissue on imaging and no T cells on flow cytometry. B and NK cell counts are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive treatment of the immunodeficiency?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gene therapy on autologous hematopoietic stem cells

explanation.summary: Complete DiGeorge syndrome, with a completely absent thymus and no T cells, may warrant a thymus transplant.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fewer than 5% of patients with DGS have complete DGS, meaning a completely absent thymus and therefore no T cells. Because the thymus is the site of T cell development, replacing it is the definitive treatment; the brick states that for patients with complete DGS a thymus transplant may be warranted, and the summary notes that DiGeorge is treated primarily by thymic transplant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ADA enzyme replacement is specific to ADA-deficient SCID and has no role in DiGeorge syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gene therapy on patient HSCs is described for ADA-SCID to replace mutated ADA; it does not address an absent thymus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HSCT is the definitive treatment for SCID, where the defect is in the hematopoietic cells themselves; in DGS the stem cells are normal but lack a thymus in which to mature.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immunoglobulin replacement is a supportive measure in partial DGS depending on infection burden; it does not restore T cell development in complete DGS.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 4-month-old boy has failure to thrive, persistent oral thrush, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. A complete blood count shows lymphopenia, and flow cytometry shows absent T cells. Before the diagnosis of severe combined immunodeficiency is established, which of the following must be excluded?

explanation.summary: HIV infection must be ruled out in any infant being evaluated for SCID.
explanation.whyCorrect: SCID should be suspected in an infant with a family history of immunodeficiency, absent lymphoid tissues, and early onset of recurrent opportunistic and viral infections with poor weight gain. The brick specifies that HIV infection needs to be ruled out, since it can also produce T cell loss and opportunistic infections in infancy; the case conclusion likewise recommends HIV screening before attributing findings to an IEI.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CMCC presents in childhood with chronic Candida infections and endocrinopathy; it does not produce absent T cells and is not a mimic that must be excluded before diagnosing SCID.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytomegalovirus is one of the opportunistic pathogens that infect T cell-deficient patients; it is a consequence, not an alternative cause, of the T cell loss.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fetal alcohol syndrome is associated with THI, not with absent T cells and Pneumocystis pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: THI is a low IgG with normal B cell numbers in an otherwise healthy infant; it does not cause lymphopenia, absent T cells, or opportunistic infections.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A newborn boy has hypocalcemia, an interrupted aortic arch, hypertelorism, micrognathia, and a cleft palate. A chest radiograph shows no thymic shadow. Fluorescence in situ hybridization for the 22q11 microdeletion is negative. Which of the following is the most accurate conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DiGeorge syndrome is excluded, and X-linked SCID should be evaluated instead

choices.label: B
choices.text: DiGeorge syndrome remains the diagnosis; it is clinical with other genetic causes

choices.label: C
choices.text: The findings indicate ataxia telangiectasia, which also causes great vessel defects

choices.label: D
choices.text: The findings indicate complete DiGeorge syndrome caused by an AIRE gene mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: The negative result supports transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy instead

explanation.summary: DiGeorge syndrome is a clinical diagnosis; 22q11 FISH can confirm it, but other genetic defects can also cause DGS.
explanation.whyCorrect: An infant with craniofacial abnormalities, great vessel defects, or hypocalcemia should be evaluated for DGS. Genetic testing with a 22q11 FISH probe can lead to a definitive diagnosis, although DGS is a clinical diagnosis, and other genetic defects besides microdeletion of chromosome 22 can lead to DGS. This infant has the full clinical picture, so a negative FISH result does not exclude DGS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A negative FISH does not exclude DGS; moreover X-linked SCID does not cause hypocalcemia, cardiac anomalies, or craniofacial malformations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ataxia telangiectasia presents with ataxia and telangiectasias in early childhood, not neonatal hypocalcemia and great vessel defects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: AIRE mutations cause chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, not DiGeorge syndrome; complete DGS refers to a completely absent thymus, which is not established by these findings alone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: THI is a low IgG with normal B cells in an infant; it has no relationship to cardiac, craniofacial, or parathyroid abnormalities.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A chest radiograph of a 2-week-old boy obtained for tachypnea shows no thymic shadow. He has no dysmorphic features, and his serum calcium concentration is normal. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of this radiographic finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Establishes the diagnosis of DiGeorge syndrome without further testing

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excludes severe combined immunodeficiency as a cause of infections

choices.label: C
choices.text: Indicates a B cell maturation defect such as X-linked agammaglobulinemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Raises suspicion for a T cell deficiency but is not specific for DiGeorge

choices.label: E
choices.text: Represents a normal finding, because the thymus is not visible in infancy

explanation.summary: An absent thymic shadow raises suspicion for a T cell deficiency but is not diagnostic of DiGeorge syndrome, because other IEIs such as SCID also lack a thymic shadow.
explanation.whyCorrect: A thymic shadow is normally seen on an infant chest x-ray. Although not diagnostic of DGS, an absent thymic shadow raises suspicion for a T cell deficiency. The brick explicitly notes that DiGeorge syndrome is not the only IEI that presents with loss of a thymic shadow; X-linked SCID, for example, also has no thymic shadow. Evaluation should proceed with a CBC, Ig levels, and T and B cell counts.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DGS is a clinical diagnosis supported by 22q11 FISH; an absent thymic shadow alone is explicitly described as not diagnostic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: SCID is one of the IEIs that presents with loss of the thymic shadow, so the finding heightens rather than excludes that concern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: XLA is a B cell disorder with normal T cells; it is associated with reduced tonsils and lymph nodes, not an absent thymus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thymic shadow is normally present on an infant chest x-ray, so its absence is abnormal.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 3-month-old boy with X-linked SCID has absent T cells, absent NK cells, and normal numbers of B cells. Loss of signaling through which of the following cytokine receptors best explains the absence of NK cells in this patient?

explanation.summary: The common gamma chain is part of the IL-15 receptor, and NK cells require IL-15 signaling for development.
explanation.whyCorrect: The IL2RG gene encodes the gamma chain of the IL-2 receptor, which is also part of the heterodimeric IL-15, IL-4, and IL-7 receptors and is therefore called the common gamma chain. NK cells require IL-15 for development, so a defect in the common gamma chain eliminates IL-15 signaling and results in absent NK cells, alongside absent T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The IFN-gamma receptor does not use the common gamma chain; decreased IFN-gamma production is a feature of CMCC.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-2 signaling is required for T cell growth; it is not the cytokine the brick assigns to NK cell development.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-4 (with IL-15) is required for B cell proliferation and differentiation into plasma cells, explaining dysfunctional B cells, not absent NK cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IL-7 signaling is required for T cell development, which explains the absent T cells rather than the absent NK cells.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 5-month-old girl has had persistent oral thrush, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, and chronic diarrhea with failure to thrive. Flow cytometry shows near-absent CD4+ T cells, present CD8+ T cells, normal B cell numbers, and normal NK cell numbers. Her B cells and monocytes do not express MHC class II molecules. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Bare lymphocyte syndrome II lacks MHC II expression, so CD4+ T cells are not generated; it presents like X-linked SCID but with normal NK cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: MHC proteins are critical for positive selection of developing T cells. In bare lymphocyte syndrome II, MHC II is not expressed, so double-positive thymocytes cannot be positively selected into CD4+ T cells. Clinically BLS II presents as X-linked SCID, although laboratory tests show normal levels of NK cells, which distinguishes the two.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ADA deficiency eliminates T, B, and NK cells and causes neutropenia; B and NK cells here are normal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: BLS I is a lack of MHC I, which prevents positive selection of CD8+ T cells; this patient has CD8+ T cells and lacks CD4+ T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RAG deficiency prevents formation of both TCRs and BCRs, so T and B cells are absent; this patient has normal B cells and present CD8+ T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: X-linked SCID eliminates both T and NK cells because the common gamma chain is required for both lineages; NK cells here are normal and MHC II expression is not affected.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 6-month-old girl whose newborn screen showed markedly reduced T cell receptor excision circles has an older brother with ataxia telangiectasia. She has received her routine 2- and 4-month vaccinations. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to evaluate her humoral immune function at this age?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fluorescence in situ hybridization probe for the 22q11 region

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgG antibody titers against the vaccines she has received

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intradermal Candida antigen skin test with induration measured

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mitogen proliferation assay of peripheral blood lymphocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum adenosine deaminase enzyme activity measurement

explanation.summary: In ataxia telangiectasia, many patients show loss of TRECs at neonatal screening, and by 6 months of age antibody responses to received vaccines can be tested.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many patients with ataxia telangiectasia display a loss of TRECs at the neonatal screen. By 6 months of age, patients can be tested for appropriate antibody responses to vaccines, meaning the presence of IgG to any vaccines received. Reduced vaccine responses reflect the impaired B cell development caused by insufficient DNA repair during V(D)J recombination; definitive diagnosis is by genetic testing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 22q11 FISH is the genetic test for DiGeorge syndrome, which is not suggested by this family history.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The Candida skin test measures the T cell inflammatory response to Candida antigens and is used to evaluate CMCC, not humoral function in AT.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mitogen proliferation studies assess lymphocyte (T cell) function, not antibody production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ADA enzyme activity evaluates ADA-deficient SCID, which is not the concern in a sibling of a patient with ataxia telangiectasia.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A state newborn screening program uses the TREC assay to identify infants with severe combined immunodeficiency. This assay detects which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inflammation at the site of intradermal Candida antigen injection

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lymphocyte proliferation in response to mitogen stimulation in vitro

choices.label: C
choices.text: Microdeletion of chromosome 22q11 by fluorescence in situ hybridization

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum IgG concentrations below 400 mg/dL in the first months of life

choices.label: E
choices.text: Small DNA circles excised from T cell genomes during V(D)J recombination

explanation.summary: The TREC assay checks for the small circles of DNA excised from T cell genomes during V(D)J recombination, which are absent when T cells are not being produced.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the United States, all states now screen for SCID using the TREC assay. The assay checks for the presence of small circles of DNA that are removed from T cell genomes during V(D)J recombination. Because these excision circles are generated only when T cells rearrange their receptors, their absence indicates a failure of T cell production, as in SCID.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Measuring inflammation after Candida antigen injection is the Candida skin test used in evaluating CMCC.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mitogen proliferation studies are a separate functional test performed during further evaluation of SCID.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 22q11 FISH is the genetic test used for DiGeorge syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An IgG below 400 mg/dL is the threshold for transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy, measured by quantitative immunoglobulin levels, not by the TREC assay.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 3-week-old boy is found to have SCID after an abnormal newborn TREC screen and confirmatory flow cytometry. He is currently asymptomatic. The immunology team recommends proceeding to hematopoietic stem cell transplantation as soon as a donor is identified rather than waiting for symptoms to develop. Which of the following best supports this recommendation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adenosine deaminase enzyme replacement loses efficacy after 3 months

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maternal IgG blocks engraftment of donor stem cells after 3 months of age

choices.label: C
choices.text: The thymus involutes at 4 months, preventing donor T cell maturation

choices.label: D
choices.text: The TREC assay becomes unreliable once the infant is older than 3 months

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transplant success is much higher before 3 months of age than after 4 months

explanation.summary: Newborn SCID screening exists in part because HSCT has a much higher success rate when performed before 3 months of age than after 4 months.
explanation.whyCorrect: Management of SCID involves early recognition due to the high morbidity and mortality associated with any form of SCID, and definitive treatment for all SCID requires hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. One reason newborn SCID screening is done is that HSCTs have a much higher success rate when performed prior to 3 months of age than when performed after 4 months of age, which is why transplantation is pursued promptly in an asymptomatic screen-positive infant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ADA replacement therapy is a bridge to HSCT for ADA-SCID; the brick does not describe a loss of efficacy at 3 months, and the timing rationale applies to all forms of SCID.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Transplacental maternal IgG wanes over time and may keep Ig levels normal initially; the brick does not describe it as blocking engraftment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick attributes the benefit to age at transplant, not to thymic involution at 4 months.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The TREC assay is a newborn screen; its reliability at older ages is not the stated reason for early transplantation.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 2-month-old girl has SCID due to adenosine deaminase deficiency, with absent T, B, and NK cells and neutropenia. No suitable stem cell donor has yet been identified. Which of the following therapies is available specifically for her form of SCID to bridge the interval until transplantation?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immunosuppressive therapy to control autoreactive T cells

explanation.summary: ADA-SCID can be treated with ADA replacement therapy until HSCT is feasible, and some centers offer gene therapy on patient HSCs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Definitive treatment for all SCID requires HSCT, but ADA-SCID uniquely can be treated with ADA replacement therapy until an HSCT is feasible. Replacing the enzyme allows breakdown of the toxic metabolites of V(D)J recombination that otherwise kill high-turnover hematopoietic cells. Some clinics can also perform gene therapy on patient HSCs to replace mutated ADA with unmutated ADA.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Endocrine replacement therapy addresses the endocrine insufficiencies of CMCC, not SCID.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunoglobulin replacement is part of supportive management for all forms of SCID and is not specific to ADA deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immunosuppressants are used in CMCC for autoimmunity; ADA-SCID lacks T cells entirely.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thymus transplant is the treatment for complete DiGeorge syndrome, where the thymus is absent; it does not correct an enzyme defect in hematopoietic cells.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 6-week-old boy with a family history of an infant death from overwhelming infection has lymphopenia and absent T cells on flow cytometry. Quantitative immunoglobulin levels are within the normal range for age. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of the immunoglobulin result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It confirms that immunoglobulin replacement therapy is unnecessary

choices.label: B
choices.text: It excludes SCID and points instead to an isolated T cell disorder

choices.label: C
choices.text: It indicates that his own B cells are producing antibody normally

choices.label: D
choices.text: It reflects transplacental maternal IgG and does not exclude SCID

choices.label: E
choices.text: It suggests transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy instead of SCID

explanation.summary: In SCID, Ig levels may be normal initially because of transplacental IgG, but they wane over time.
explanation.whyCorrect: Initial evaluation for SCID involves a CBC with differential, enumeration of B and T cell subsets, and quantitative Ig levels. Lymphopenia and absence of T cells are expected. Ig levels may be normal initially due to transplacental IgG, but the level will wane over time, so a normal Ig result at 6 weeks does not argue against SCID in an infant with absent T cells and a suggestive family history.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ig replacement together with prophylactic antifungals and antibiotics is necessary in SCID management, since the maternal IgG will wane.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Normal Ig in early infancy is expected in SCID because of maternal IgG; it cannot be used to exclude the diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The measured IgG is maternal in origin; without T cells, the infant's own B cells cannot receive T cell help and are dysfunctional regardless of the level.
whyWrongByChoice.E: THI is diagnosed when IgG is below 400 mg/dL with normal B cell numbers in an infant without a T cell defect; this infant has normal Ig and absent T cells.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis due to a confirmed AIRE mutation is treated with calcium and vitamin D for hypoparathyroidism. Her adrenal function is currently normal. Which of the following best describes her risk of adrenal failure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is present in about 30% at presentation and rarely develops later

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is prevented by prophylactic antifungal therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is unlikely because AIRE loss affects only the parathyroid glands

choices.label: D
choices.text: It occurs only in patients who lack hypoparathyroidism

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most patients develop it by age 15, so ongoing monitoring is needed

explanation.summary: In CMCC, adrenal failure is present in only 5% at presentation but develops in more than 60% of patients by age 15.
explanation.whyCorrect: Loss of T cell central tolerance in AIRE deficiency often results in endocrine insufficiencies. Hypoparathyroidism is the most common, present in 30% of patients at presentation. Adrenal failure occurs in 5% of patients at presentation, but more than 60% of cases develop it by age 15, so a currently normal adrenal axis does not remove the need for surveillance and eventual endocrine replacement therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thirty percent at presentation is the figure for hypoparathyroidism; adrenal failure is present in only 5% at presentation and most often develops later.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Prophylactic antifungals treat the Candida infections; autoimmunity is addressed with immunosuppressants and endocrine replacement, not antifungals.
whyWrongByChoice.C: AIRE loss allows autoreactive T cells to escape against many tissue-restricted antigens, producing multiple endocrine insufficiencies, not just parathyroid disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both endocrine insufficiencies arise from autoreactive T cells and can coexist; hypoparathyroidism does not protect against adrenal failure.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: T cells from a 6-year-old boy with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis are stimulated in vitro. Compared with T cells from a healthy control, decreased production of which of the following would be expected?

explanation.summary: Loss of AIRE causes T cell dysfunction with decreased production of IL-2 and IFN-gamma.
explanation.whyCorrect: A loss of AIRE causes three important immune effects: failure to express tissue-restricted antigens in the thymic medulla (impairing central tolerance), reduced expression of the pattern recognition receptor Dectin-1, and T cell dysfunction including decreased production of IL-2 and IFN-gamma. The summary attributes the immunodeficiency of CMCC to the loss of IL-2, IFN-gamma, and Dectin-1.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-7 is a developmental cytokine for T cells, not a product whose secretion is reduced in CMCC.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-4 is not among the cytokines the brick identifies as decreased in CMCC; the pair is IL-2 and IFN-gamma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-4 and IL-15 are cytokines B cells require for proliferation and differentiation; they signal through the common gamma chain and are not the cytokines reduced in CMCC.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IL-7 and IL-15 drive T and NK cell development through the common gamma chain; their loss of signaling defines X-linked SCID.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl with ataxia telangiectasia has recurrent sinopulmonary infections. Laboratory studies show reduced numbers of both T and B cells and low IgG responses to prior vaccinations. Which of the following best explains why a defect in the ATM gene impairs lymphocyte development?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DNA breaks made during V(D)J recombination are not detected and repaired

choices.label: B
choices.text: Signals downstream of the B cell receptor are not transmitted

choices.label: C
choices.text: The common gamma chain needed for IL-7 and IL-15 signaling is absent

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tissue-restricted self-antigens are not expressed in the thymic medulla

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toxic metabolites of V(D)J recombination accumulate in dividing lymphocytes

explanation.summary: ATM detects and repairs DNA damage; because DNA is broken and repaired during V(D)J recombination, ATM loss affects both T and B cell development to varying degrees.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ataxia telangiectasia is caused by autosomal recessive mutations in ATM, which is responsible for detection and repair of DNA damage and regulation of cell cycle genes such as p53 and BRCA1. Because DNA is broken and repaired in V(D)J recombination, a loss of ATM can affect both T and B cell development to various degrees, explaining reduced TRECs, reduced vaccine responses, and immunodeficiency in roughly half of patients.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Failure of BCR signal transmission is the Btk defect of XLA, which affects only B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Absence of the common gamma chain is the mechanism of X-linked SCID and causes absent T and NK cells with present B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Failure to express tissue-restricted antigens in the thymic medulla is the mechanism of AIRE deficiency in CMCC.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Accumulation of toxic metabolites from V(D)J recombination is the mechanism of ADA deficiency, not of ATM loss.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 13-month-old boy is brought in with his fourth episode of bacterial pneumonia and several weeks of watery diarrhea. A maternal uncle died of infection in infancy. Laboratory studies show elevated serum IgM with very low IgG, IgA, and IgE, and an absolute neutropenia. Flow cytometry shows that his activated T cells fail to express a key costimulatory surface molecule. Which of the following molecules is most likely defective?

explanation.summary: X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome results from a CD40L mutation that blocks class switching.
explanation.whyCorrect: X-HIMS, the most common form of hyper-IgM syndrome, is caused by an X-linked mutation in CD40L. Without CD40L on T cells binding CD40 on B cells, B cells cannot enter the germinal center to class switch, so IgM stays high while IgG, IgA, and IgE are low. Because CD40 is also on macrophages, patients get opportunistic and intracellular infections, and roughly 65% have neutropenia, matching this male infant with a suggestive family history.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Interferon-gamma receptor defects cause MSMD, presenting with mycobacterial infections and normal immunoglobulin levels.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The polymeric Ig receptor transcytoses IgA across mucosa and is relevant to the redundancy seen in IgA deficiency, not to a class-switching defect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: STAT3 defects cause hyper-IgE syndrome, with elevated IgE, cold abscesses, and coarse facies, not high IgM with low IgG.
whyWrongByChoice.E: WASP mutations cause Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, characterized by thrombocytopenia and eczema, not this immunoglobulin pattern.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with a history of recurrent sinus infections develops flushing, wheezing, and a drop in blood pressure a few minutes into her first-ever blood transfusion. Prior testing had shown an isolated low serum IgA with normal IgG, IgM, and IgE. Which of the following is the most appropriate measure to prevent this reaction with future transfusions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Administer prophylactic antibiotics before each transfusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Give supplemental IgA before the transfusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfuse only IgA-deficient or washed blood products

explanation.summary: Selective IgA deficiency can cause transfusion anaphylaxis via anti-IgA antibodies, prevented with IgA-deficient or washed blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because these patients make little or no IgA, they may not be tolerant to it; after sensitization they can form anti-IgA antibodies and react to the IgA in donor blood, producing anaphylaxis. The brick specifically advises using blood products with caution and giving IgA-deficient or washed blood products to minimize this risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Prophylactic antibiotics address recurrent infections, not an anaphylactic transfusion reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Giving IgA would provide more of the very antigen the patient reacts to and could worsen anaphylaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Selective IgA deficiency usually requires no treatment and is not an indication for stem cell transplant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgG replacement does not remove the IgA in donor blood or the patient's anti-IgA antibodies, so it does not prevent the reaction.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy has recurrent skin abscesses that are notably nontender and lack surrounding warmth or redness, along with chronic eczema and recurrent pneumonias. On exam he has a broad nose, prominent lower lip, and retained primary teeth. Serum IgE is 3,500 IU/mL with peripheral eosinophilia. A defect in which of the following best explains his condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD40 ligand on activated T cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: ICOS on follicular helper T cells

explanation.summary: Hyper-IgE syndrome is an autosomal dominant STAT3 defect that impairs Th17 development.
explanation.whyCorrect: HIES is caused by a STAT3 defect, and STAT3 is required to differentiate naive T cells into Th17. Loss of Th17 impairs IL-17-driven neutrophil recruitment, producing cold abscesses, while the Th2/IgE axis is elevated. STAT3 is also needed for bone development, explaining the coarse facies, retained baby teeth, and fractures, and diagnosis rests on markedly elevated IgE plus eosinophilia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD40L defects cause X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome, with high IgM and low IgG, not elevated IgE with cold abscesses.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ICOS mutations are associated with CVID, causing low IgG rather than markedly elevated IgE.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interferon-gamma receptor defects cause MSMD, with mycobacterial infections rather than this triad.
whyWrongByChoice.E: WASP mutations cause Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (thrombocytopenia, eczema, bleeding), not cold abscesses, high IgE, or coarse facies.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 10-month-old boy has prolonged bleeding after circumcision, scattered petechiae, chronic eczema, and recurrent otitis media and pneumonia. His platelet count is 40,000/microliter with a low mean platelet volume. A maternal uncle had similar problems as a child. Which of the following proteins is most likely mutated?

explanation.summary: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked WASP defect presenting with thrombocytopenia, immunodeficiency, and eczema.
explanation.whyCorrect: WAS is an X-linked loss-of-function mutation in WASP, a protein expressed exclusively in hematopoietic cells that is critical for actin polymerization. This produces the classic triad of thrombocytopenia (with small, few platelets), immunodeficiency, and eczema, along with bruising, bleeding, and petechiae, and the male sex with affected maternal relatives fits X-linked inheritance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD40L defects cause X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome, defined by an abnormal immunoglobulin pattern rather than low platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ICOS/ICOSL defects are linked to CVID, an antibody-production disorder, not a platelet and actin defect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interferon-gamma receptor defects cause MSMD with mycobacterial infections and normal platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.D: STAT3 defects cause hyper-IgE syndrome with cold abscesses and high IgE, not thrombocytopenia.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy from a country that gives BCG vaccine at birth developed a disseminated infection with the vaccine strain in the weeks after vaccination, and later a nontuberculous Mycobacterium avium infection. His B cell, T cell, and immunoglobulin levels are normal, and HIV testing is negative. A defect in which of the following pathways best explains his susceptibility?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD40L-CD40 interaction required for B-cell class switching

choices.label: B
choices.text: Class switching of activated B cells to IgA

choices.label: D
choices.text: The IL-12/IFN-gamma axis needed for Th1 responses

explanation.summary: MSMD arises from IL-12 receptor or IFN-gamma receptor defects that impair Th1 and macrophage activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: MSMD is caused by loss-of-function mutations along the Th1 activation pathway, most often in the IL-12 receptor beta chain or the IFN-gamma receptors. IL-12 and IFN-gamma drive Th1 differentiation, and Th1-derived IFN-gamma is critical for macrophage activation; losing this leaves patients susceptible to weakly virulent intracellular mycobacteria such as BCG and nontuberculous species, while B cell, T cell, and immunoglobulin levels remain normal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD40L-CD40 defects cause X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome, with an abnormal immunoglobulin pattern rather than isolated mycobacterial disease and normal Ig levels.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An IgA class-switching defect causes selective IgA deficiency, which presents with mucosal bacterial infections, not disseminated mycobacterial disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: STAT3/Th17 defects cause hyper-IgE syndrome with cold abscesses and elevated IgE, not selective mycobacterial susceptibility.
whyWrongByChoice.E: WASP defects cause Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome with thrombocytopenia and eczema, not this mycobacterial picture.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman has had recurrent sinus and lung infections over several years and now has bronchiectasis and an autoimmune cytopenia. Laboratory studies show a low IgG together with a low IgA, while her B cell and T cell counts are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: CVID presents in adults with low IgG plus low IgA and/or IgM, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, and autoimmunity.
explanation.whyCorrect: CVID is the second most common IEI in adults (about 1:25,000) and is defined by a loss of IgG with additional loss of IgA or IgM from defective plasma cell production. Patients typically present between ages 20 and 40 with sinus, lung, and GI infections plus autoimmune and inflammatory disease, and chronic lung disease with bronchiectasis is a major complication, exactly matching this patient with normal B and T cell counts.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hyper-IgE syndrome is defined by markedly elevated IgE with cold abscesses, not low IgG and IgA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Selective IgA deficiency shows an isolated low IgA with normal IgG, whereas this patient also has low IgG.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome presents in male infants with thrombocytopenia and eczema, not adult-onset hypogammaglobulinemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome shows high IgM with low IgG and presents in male infants, not an adult woman.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A patient with STAT3-deficient hyper-IgE syndrome repeatedly forms skin abscesses that lack the usual warmth, redness, pain, and swelling. Which of the following best explains why these abscesses are 'cold'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A markedly low platelet count blunts the inflammatory response

choices.label: B
choices.text: Absent CD40 ligand prevents B-cell class switching

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deficient interferon-gamma signaling prevents macrophage activation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Excess IgE triggers mast cell degranulation at the abscess site

choices.label: E
choices.text: Failure to generate Th17 cells impairs neutrophil recruitment

explanation.summary: In HIES, loss of Th17 cells prevents IL-17-mediated neutrophil recruitment, producing inflammation-poor 'cold' abscesses.
explanation.whyCorrect: STAT3 is required for Th17 differentiation, and Th17 cells secrete IL-17 to recruit neutrophils to sites of extracellular bacterial and fungal infection. Without neutrophil recruitment the infection is walled off in an abscess that lacks the heat, redness, pain, and swelling of normal inflammation, which is why HIES abscesses are described as 'cold.'

whyWrongByChoice.A: Low platelets are the hallmark of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and cause bleeding, not cold abscesses.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Absent CD40L is the defect in X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome and affects antibody class switching, not neutrophil-driven inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Deficient IFN-gamma/macrophage activation defines MSMD and its mycobacterial infections, not the cold abscesses of HIES.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Although IgE is elevated in HIES, mast cell degranulation is not the mechanism of the cold abscesses; absent neutrophil recruitment is.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man is found on routine testing to have an isolated low serum IgA with normal IgG, IgM, and IgE. He has had no serious infections. Which of the following best explains why he is asymptomatic despite his IgA deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He compensates by producing elevated levels of IgE

choices.label: B
choices.text: His neutrophil count is markedly increased

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgG is transcytosed across mucosa in place of IgA

explanation.summary: Most patients with selective IgA deficiency are asymptomatic because redundant mechanisms, including IgM secretion via the pIgR, compensate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Selective IgA deficiency is the most common adaptive IEI (incidence up to about 1:100), and most patients are asymptomatic. The relative lack of IgA is offset by redundant immune mechanisms: the polymeric Ig receptor normally transcytoses secretory IgA, and IgM can also bind the pIgR and be secreted into the mucosal lumen, providing backup mucosal protection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Elevated IgE is a feature of hyper-IgE syndrome and does not substitute for mucosal IgA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The compensation is antibody-based redundancy at the mucosa, not an increase in neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Overproduction of IFN-gamma is not a compensatory mechanism described for IgA deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick attributes the redundancy specifically to IgM binding the pIgR, not to IgG being transcytosed in place of IgA.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A boy with X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome develops Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and Cryptosporidium diarrhea in addition to recurrent pyogenic bacterial infections. Beyond the failure of B-cell class switching, which of the following mechanisms best explains his susceptibility to these opportunistic and intracellular organisms?

choices.label: B
choices.text: An IL-12 receptor mutation prevents Th1 differentiation

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD40L is also required to fully activate macrophages

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of secretory IgA weakens the mucosal barrier

explanation.summary: CD40 is also on macrophages, so CD40L loss impairs macrophage activation and causes opportunistic infections in X-HIMS.
explanation.whyCorrect: CD40 is found on macrophages as well as B cells. CD40L, together with IFN-gamma, provides the full stimulation needed to activate macrophages. Because X-HIMS patients lack functional CD40L, they cannot fully activate macrophages and become susceptible to opportunistic and intracellular infections in addition to encapsulated bacterial infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Absent WASP causes the platelet and immune defects of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, not the CD40L defect here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-12 receptor mutations cause MSMD; the defect in this patient is CD40L, which also impairs macrophage activation via a different route.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of secretory IgA is the mechanism in selective IgA deficiency, which does not explain opportunistic macrophage-dependent infections.
whyWrongByChoice.E: STAT3/Th17 failure is the mechanism of hyper-IgE syndrome, not X-HIMS.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with common variable immunodeficiency is maintained on immunoglobulin replacement. In addition to bronchiectasis, which of the following malignancies is he at increased risk of developing and should be monitored for?

explanation.summary: CVID carries an increased risk of malignancy, especially non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: An important cause of morbidity and mortality in CVID is chronic lung disease, especially bronchiectasis, which affects 30 to 50 percent of patients. In addition, CVID patients are at increased risk of malignancy, especially non-Hodgkin lymphoma, so long-term monitoring for both bronchiectasis and lymphoma is recommended.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic myeloid leukemia is not the malignancy CVID patients are noted to be at risk for.
